title: Site contract and scope
audience: Commercial cleaners and supervisors who agree a site contract and its scope.
learningOutcomes: Identify the contract scope, exclusions, frequencies and the people who authorise changes.
Record variations in writing before the work changes.
Refuse to promise work that the contract does not include.

instruction.heading: Reading the contract
instruction.body: The contract sets the scope of the work. It names the areas, the tasks, the frequencies, the standards, the exclusions and the people who may authorise changes. Read it before you price the work or start it, and read the attached scope schedule as part of the contract, not as a separate note. Look hard at the exclusions. A missing or vague exclusion is the most common cause of disputes, because the site and the cleaner remember different things about what was agreed. Words such as as required, periodic, regular or as needed do not give a frequency, so ask the contract owner to replace them with a number of visits or a cycle before work starts. Check who signs for the client, who receives service reports and who can approve a change. A person who can request work is not always a person who can approve it. Where a standard is named, check how it will be measured, for example by a checklist or an inspection, so the standard can be shown to have been met.

instruction.heading: Variations
instruction.body: A variation is any change to the agreed scope. That includes an extra area, a different product, a different frequency, a new task, a change of time that affects the price, or a removal of work the business has agreed to do. Record each variation in writing. Describe the change, the reason it was asked for, the time and product it needs, the price, and the person the contract names as the approver. Get that approval before the extra work starts. A verbal request from a site staff member is a request, not a variation, even when the request is reasonable and the staff member has authority within the building. Note the request, tell the staff member that it needs to go to the contract owner, and send it through that route. Where a contract allows approval to be given after work has started, follow the wording of that contract, and record the approval when it is given. Keep the variation register in the same file as the contract so that the current scope can be read in one place.

instruction.heading: Promises and representations
instruction.body: Do not promise work, results or standards that the contract does not include. Saying the stain will never return, that a room will be dust-free for a week, or that the business will add a service next month are all statements about what the business will do or achieve. The ACCC's guidance says that claims about services must be accurate and based on reasonable grounds, and that a business must be able to back up what it says when it makes the claim. Predictions about the future also need reasonable grounds at the time they are made, and the business should allow for uncertainty. Misleading impressions count, even where they were not intended. When a request falls outside the contract, explain what the contract covers in plain terms, and refer the request to the contract owner. Keep the wording factual: say what is included, rather than guarantee what the result will be.

instruction.heading: Keeping the records together
instruction.body: A contract is only useful if the current scope can be found quickly. Keep the signed contract, the scope schedule, every approved variation, the approval for each one, and the service reports in one file. When a variation is approved, update the scope schedule, the checklist and the staff briefing so that they match. Mark old versions as superseded rather than deleting them, so that the history can be shown if a dispute arises. The file is also the first place to look when a new team member asks what they should be doing on a site.

procedure: Read the scope, exclusions, frequencies, standards and the people who authorise changes, including the attached schedule.
Ask the contract owner to replace any vague frequency or standard with a measurable term before work starts.
Note any request outside the scope, and refer it to the approver named in the contract.
Record each approved variation in writing with its price, time and product implications, and get approval before the extra work starts.
Do not promise work or results outside the contract, and explain what the contract covers in plain terms.
Keep the contract, the schedule, the variations and the approvals together, and mark superseded versions.

workedExamples.situation: A site staff member asks for the carpets to be cleaned, which the contract excludes.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you say, and what do you record?
workedExamples.reasoning: Explain that carpets are excluded under the contract, and that the business cannot take them on without an approved variation. Record the request, the name of the person who made it, the time and the area. Refer it to the contract owner for a written variation and a price. Do not start the carpets, and do not say that they will be done later.

workedExamples.situation: A tenant's manager tells a cleaner in the corridor that the windows on the top floor should be added this week, and that the business will be paid for it later.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Is this a variation, and can the cleaner agree to it?
workedExamples.reasoning: It is not a variation until it is written, priced and approved by the named person. The cleaner should not agree to it, and should not promise a date or a price. Note the request, confirm it in writing to the contract owner, and say that the business will reply once the request has been assessed. The promise about later payment is outside the cleaner's authority.

workedExamples.situation: The contract says the common areas are cleaned on a monthly deep-clean cycle. The site manager asks to move the cycle to weekly.
workedExamples.reasoning: A change of frequency is a variation. Send the request to the contract owner with the time and product implications, and the price, for approval. Do not change the cycle at the door, and do not confirm the new cycle to the site staff until the approval is in writing. Until then, the current contract applies.

equipmentAndPpe: Variation request form, with price, time and product fields.
List of named approvers for the site, held by the supervisor.
No PPE is required for the desk work in this lesson. Site PPE applies when you visit a site.

commonErrors.error: Doing work the contract excludes because the site asked.
commonErrors.prevention: Refer the request to a written, priced variation before any work.
Read the exclusions as carefully as the inclusions, and ask about any gap.

commonErrors.error: Accepting a verbal variation from a staff member who has no approval authority.
commonErrors.prevention: Note the request, and send it to the approver named in the contract.

commonErrors.error: Promising results, dates or prices the contract does not cover.
commonErrors.prevention: State what the contract includes, and refer anything else to the contract owner.

commonErrors.error: Working from a scope schedule that has not been updated after a variation.
commonErrors.prevention: Update the schedule, checklist and briefing as soon as a variation is approved.

commonErrors.error: Accepting vague frequencies such as as required or regular.
commonErrors.prevention: Ask the contract owner for a measurable frequency before work starts.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Claims about the business's services must be accurate and based on reasonable grounds. Forward-looking claims need reasonable grounds when they are made. The ACCC states that misleading impressions count even where they were not intended (ACCC, page dated 28 June 2026).
The contract itself governs variations, and the contract owner or a qualified adviser should be asked where the terms are unclear.
This lesson is general guidance on handling a service contract. It is not legal advice and does not give any authority to vary a contract.

qualityStandard: Scope, inclusions and exclusions identified from a sample contract, with every vague frequency or standard flagged.
Verbal variation request in the case study referred for written, priced approval, with no work started.
No excluded work performed and no result, date or price promised outside the contract.
Variation register and approval record complete for each change in the case study.
documentationEvidence: Contract scope record listing inclusions, exclusions, frequencies, standards and named approvers.
Variation request with the change, reason, time, product, price and approver.
Approval record dated before the extra work starts.
Service report or communication log showing what was promised, if anything, and who was told.
summary: Read the exclusions as carefully as the inclusions.
Variations are written, priced and approved by the named person before any work starts.
Do not promise what the contract does not include, and avoid guarantees.
Keep the contract, schedule, variations and approvals together and current.

knowledgeChecks.question: A site staff member asks for excluded carpets to be cleaned. What is correct?
options: Clean them because the site asked, and sort out the paperwork later
Refer the request for a written, priced variation before any work
Ignore the request and say nothing to the site or the supervisor

knowledgeChecks.question: What is often the source of disputes?
options: Too many inclusions in the price

knowledgeChecks.question: Is a verbal request from a site staff member a variation?
options: Yes, if it is urgent and the site staff member is senior enough to decide for the site
Yes, once the cleaner agrees to it and the time is recorded in the log book for the site
No, a variation is written, priced and approved by the named person before the work starts

knowledgeChecks.question: Should a worker promise work, results or standards that the contract does not include?
options: Yes, to keep the client happy
Yes, if the site staff ask for it
No. Do not promise work, results or standards that the contract does not include
